Different levels of visual perceptual skills are associated with specific modifications in functional connectivity and global efficiency

International Journal of Psychophysiology 123 (2018) 127–135
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2017.10.002

Sabrina Danti, Giacomo Handjaras, Luca Cecchetti, Helen Beuzeron-Mangina, Pietro Pietrini, Emiliano Ricciardi

Twenty-three young right-handed healthy subjects (13 M/10F; mean age ± s.d. = 26 ± 3 yrs) were enrolled in the study. All subjects signed a written informed consent prior to the enrolment into the study, under a protocol approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Pisa, Italy (Protocol 1616/2003).

The task of the Mangina-Test consists of identifying a simple visual stimulus that is masked (inserted) into a simultaneously presented complex configuration, according to their exact geometrical properties: size, dimension, direction, spatial orientation and shape (Fig. 1). Five runs were obtained in each fMRI session.

Responses to different stimuli were measured using blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) contrast with the acquisition of T2*- weighted gradient echo planar images (GRE-EPI) in a 1.5 T GE scanner (General Electric, Milwaukee, WI). In each time series, the whole brain volume was acquired 108 times, each volume consisting of 33 contiguous 4 mm thick axial slices (TR = 2.5 s, TE = 40 ms, FA = 90°, FOV = 24 cm, IPR = 64 × 64 voxels and 3.75 × 3.75 mm). High-resolution T1-weighted spoiled gradient recall images (SPGR) (TR = 19.58 ms, TE = 3.58 ms, flip angle = 10°, FOV = 240 mm with 0.469 × 0.469 mm in-plane resolution, 512 × 512 acquisition matrix, and 1 mm axial slice thickness) were obtained for each subject to provide detailed brain anatomy; the SPGR images were used as an anatomical underlay for the statistical maps.

Data analysis was performed using the AFNI (afni.nimh.nih.gov; Cox, 1996) and Surf Ice. After slice time correction and spatial realignment, time series for each voxel were spatially smoothed (Gaussian kernel, 6-mm, full width at half maximum) and then normalized to the mean. All the volumes of the five runs were concatenated. The images were normalized to the Talairach-Tournoux space (Talairach and Tournoux, 1988) and resampled to 1 mm3 voxels.

Previously processed data were now treated to remove nuisance signals (i.e., head movements, the polynomial regressors accounting for linear, quadratic and cubic drifts): for each subject nuisance signals were regressed out from the voxel time series (3dSynthesize). Afterwards, data were low-pass filtered (3dFourier) at 0.15 Hz to remove high frequency physiological artifacts including cardiac and respiratory pulsatility (Birn et al., 2006; Danti et al., 2010; Hallquist et al., 2013).

Individual performances ranged from 37 to 44 correct answers (mean score ± SE = 40.8 ± 1.8).

Each fMRI run contained eight stimuli pairs with two 15 s (or more, depending on response time) of rest at its onset and ending, to obtain a baseline measure of activity (270 s of total duration).

Previously processed data were now treated to remove nuisance signals
(i.e., head movements, the polynomial regressors accounting for linear,
quadratic and cubic drifts): for each subject nuisance signals were re-
gressed out from the voxel time series (3dSynthesize). Afterwards, data
were low-pass ﬁltered (3dFourier) at 0.15 Hz to remove high frequency
physiological artifacts including cardiac and respiratory pulsatility
(Birn et al., 2006; Danti et al., 2010; Hallquist et al., 2013). We deﬁned
our nodes of the network by placing a 5 mm radius sphere on the po-
sitive peak of each cluster. Each cluster was generated by the super-
imposition of average task-related positive response as deﬁned in the
one-sample t-test mask with the anatomical regions of the probabilistic
cytoarchitectonic atlas (Eickhoﬀ et al., 2005) and by including only the
resulting overlaps with a minimum volume of 2500 μL. In this way, we
obtained 40 regions of interest (ROIs) (i.e., nodes of the network), 18 in
the left hemisphere and 22 in the right side of the brain. Subsequently,
for each node, the preprocessed time series were further normalized by
using z-score transformation. For each edge between the 40 nodes, we
performed a multiple regression analysis using the PPI interaction as
regressor of interest, obtained by multiplying element-by-element the
task and the node time series, and considering the node time series and
the task as regressors of no-interest (Friston et al., 1997; O'Reilly et al.,
2012). Although PPI did not provide strong directional information (Di
et al., 2017), it is not symmetric by construct (i.e., the PPI coeﬃcient of
the ROI x used as predictor of ROI y could be diﬀerent from the PPI
coeﬃcient of the ROI y prediction on the ROI x) as opposed to other
techniques (e.g., functional connectivity performed using the correla-
tion coeﬃcient). Hence, for each subject, we used the PPI coeﬃcients to
build a non-symmetric connectivity matrix between the 40 nodes. Fi-
nally, a multiple regression analysis was performed to assess the re-
lationship between edges strength (i.e., PPI coeﬃcients) and the Man-
gina-Test score, adding subjects' RTs as nuisance variable, thus to
obtain a matrix of signiﬁcant nodes connections related to Mangina-
Test scores irrespectively from the time spent on the task (p < 0.05,
uncorrected) (Fig. 3). Moreover, a χ2 test was assessed to verify whe-
ther the nodes which showed a signiﬁcant association with the beha-
vioral score were equally distributed between the two hemispheres and
the two interhemispheric directed edges (i.e., functional connections
from the left to the right hemisphere and vice versa). The PPI pipeline
was developed in Matlab (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA) and it was
formally identical to the current voxel-wise approach used in FSL
(Smith et al., 2004).

2.8. Relationship at network level between eﬃciency measures and
behavioral performance

Here, we analyzed topological properties of the task-related func-
tional network resulted from the whole brain connectivity matrix, and
from the connectivity matrices restricted to the nodes within the left
and right hemisphere. First, in each subject, the connectivity matrix
based on the PPI coeﬃcients was thresholded to retain all the positive
values (approximately the 50th percentile of the whole PPI coeﬃcients
distribution) and to deﬁne an adjacency matrix for the subsequent
unweighted graph. Indeed, this step is crucial because the resulting
topological properties may directly depend on this threshold value
(Bullmore and Sporns, 2009). However, we selected only positive edges
to ensure a straightforward interpretation of the graph. Moreover a
central-tendency threshold (half of all possible connections) may result
in stable structures across subjects, and it was suitable to estimate to-
pological diﬀerences across conditions. In accordance with Latora and
Marchiori (Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Latora and Marchiori, 2001),
we calculated the global eﬃciency (EG) and local eﬃciency (EL) indices

as measures of functional integration between nodes in the brain and in
each hemisphere separately. Finally, multiple regression analyses were
performed to assess the relationship between the EG (p < 0.05), the EL
(p < 0.05) indices and the behavioral performance, adding subjects'
RTs as a nuisance variable (Figs. 4, 5). All the graph analyses were
accomplished with Matlab (Matworks Inc., Natick, MA, USA), and the
Brain Connectivity Toolbox (Rubinov and Sporns, 2010).

Forty nodes (18 in the left hemisphere, 22 in the right side of the
brain) were obtained by the superimposition of average task-related
positive response with the anatomical regions of the probabilistic cy-
toarchitectonic atlas (see Section 2.7). For each edge, the coeﬃcient of
the PPI analysis during the administration of the Mangina-Test was
estimated and subsequently correlated with behavioral performances
including the RTs as a covariate of no interest (p < 0.05, uncorrected)
(Fig. 3). In this analysis, only one signiﬁcant positive association was
found, connecting the right middle temporal gyrus to the right calcarine
cortex. When considering signiﬁcant negative associations only, results
highlighted 147 edges out of 1560 possible connections (p < 0.05,
uncorrected). Signiﬁcant negative edges were mainly located within the
right hemisphere (~ 40% of overall signiﬁcant edges) and in inter-
hemispheric connections from the left to the right hemisphere (~ 31%),
whereas the signiﬁcant connections from the right to the left hemi-
sphere and within the left hemisphere were relatively few (~ 17% and
~11% of overall signiﬁcant edges, respectively). This diﬀerent dis-
tribution of negative associations between the PPI connectivity index
and behavioral performance was further conﬁrmed by means of a χ2
test (χ2

3.4. Results at network level

Here, we reported the associations between the topological prop-
erties of the functional networks and the behavioral performance.
Speciﬁcally, we measured the global eﬃciency (EG) and the local eﬃ-
ciency (EL) indices as they represent diﬀerent levels of information
integration. When considering the whole-brain graph, or the one de-
ﬁned using the right hemisphere nodes only, signiﬁcant negative

associations between the EG and behavioral performance were found
(whole brain: β = − 0.427, p = 0.042; right hemisphere: β = − 0.440,
p = 0.039; 95%; Fig. 4B and D). Conversely, within the left hemisphere
no signiﬁcant association between the EG index and Mangina-Test
scores was found (β = − 0.378, p = 0.072; Fig. 4C).

For each node of the whole-brain graph, the local eﬃciency (EL)
index was correlated to the behavioral data (p < 0.05, uncorrected).
Eleven nodes, seven belonging to the right hemisphere, which com-
prised regions of occipital and frontal cortices, showed a signiﬁcant
negative association between the EL index and the Mangina-Test scores
(Fig. 5).

Here, we characterized the neural activity of a healthy sample
during a cognitive task involving disembedding ability, by correlating
the changes in neural responses to behavioral performances at various
levels of information processing, from local neural activity to network
topological properties. Our results showed: i) at voxel level, a negative
association in task-related brain areas between neural responses and
performance scores; ii) at edge level, a negative association between
PPI coeﬃcients and behavioral performances, mainly restricted to the
edges belonging to the right hemisphere and to the inter-hemispheric
connections originating from the left one; iii) at network level, a sig-
niﬁcant negative association between eﬃciency indices (i.e., global and
local) and the behavioral performance mainly in the right hemisphere.
Altogether, these results indicate that diﬀerent levels of eﬃciency

during a disembedding task are associated with speciﬁc changes in
brain responses both at a small (i.e., the neural responses at voxel level)
and large scale (i.e., the edge strength between nodes or the topological
properties of the network).

Moreover, when focusing on the network structure, the PPI coeﬃ-
cients between nodes decreased when subjects performed better. In
particular, these reductions were mainly restricted to left to right in-
terhemispheric and right intrahemispheric connections (Fig. 3). How-
ever, as the PPI coeﬃcients resulted to be positive or negative, the in-
terpretation is not straightforward, as changes in interactions between
nodes were associated with the behavioral performance, irrespectively
of the direction of nodes interaction. To clarify this issue, we re-
presented in Fig. 4A all the signiﬁcant edges (p < 0.05), showing that
they had a similar pattern, with a positive PPI coeﬃcient in the low-
performing subjects and a negative PPI coeﬃcient in the high-per-
forming ones. Speciﬁcally, the left lingual, fusiform, insular and cau-
date regions showed widespread positive interactions (i.e., positive PPI
coeﬃcients) with the right hemisphere in low-performing subjects,
whereas the same interactions are negative in high-performing in-
dividuals. Overall, these results indicate negative interactions between
nodes in the right intra- and inter-hemispheric connections in high-
performing individuals. In line with a more eﬃcient processing, these
negative interactions between visual processing regions and parietal

However, although the PPI analysis oﬀers the ability to capture ﬁne-
grained, speciﬁc diﬀerences between edges,
it is unable to catch
changes in the network properties. For instance, integrated networks
with a long-distance organization retained highly diﬀerent topological
properties, as compared to networks with a clustered organization,
regardless of diﬀerences in edges strength between the two (Bullmore
and Sporns, 2009). Thus, to further characterize the underlying phe-
nomenon of improved eﬃciency in a more comprehensive and sensible
manner, we analyzed the topological properties of the task-related
network.

At network level, the global eﬃciency index suggested that low-
performing subjects had a more integrated network, especially within
the right hemisphere. Such a network consisted of shorter paths be-
tween distant nodes that optimize the speed during the sharing of in-
formation (Ginestet et al., 2011). Moreover, when measuring topolo-
gical changes among neighbor nodes as shown by the local eﬃciency
index results, only eleven nodes out of forty (seven belonging to the
right hemisphere) showed a signiﬁcant negative association with be-
havioral results. Taken together, these pieces of evidence suggest that
cognitive eﬃciency may be adequately investigated using both global
and local measures of information (Fair et al., 2009; Giessing et al.,

We hypothesize that diﬀerent levels of Mangina-Test performance
may be associated with modiﬁcations in neural responses and con-
nectivity in task-related brain areas of healthy subjects (Mangina et al.,
2009a; Mangina et al., 2009b). In accordance with this, subjects with
higher visuo-spatial skills would perform this disembedding task more
eﬃciently, ultimately recruiting brain resources in a more parsimo-
nious manner. Consequently, we explored brain activity at diﬀerent
levels of information processing, from local responses (i.e., voxel level)
to connectivity strength between brain nodes (i.e., edge level). In ad-
dition, to further characterize the underlying phenomenon of improved
eﬃciency in a more comprehensive and sensible manner, we took into
account the topological properties of the task-related network (i.e.,
network structure level). Notably, graph theory approaches have re-
cently quantiﬁed eﬃciency in terms of the cost of transmitting in-
formation within large-scale brain networks (Bullmore and Sporns,
2009), rather than on the activity of single brain voxels. Speciﬁcally,
here we measured the local and global eﬃciency indices to quantify the
ability of the brain to integrate information during the Mangina-Test at
the local (i.e., node neighborhoods) and global level (i.e., between more
distant nodes
respectively (Latora and
Marchiori, 2001, 2003). In this framework, the concept of eﬃciency
during a visual spatial task extends beyond the small-scale level (i.e.
single node) to the large-scale brain network structure (i.e., from nodes
to edges, to motifs and hubs).
